vignette: It begins with the sound of wet asphalt giving way under weight. Arthur remembers the exact second the tires lose their grip on the rain-slicked highway. There is no time for the brake pedal to matter. The world flips, then stills, suspended in the metallic groan of crushed steel. When his vision clears, the air smells of burnt rubber and copper. His hands move before his mind catches up-reaching across the crumpled dashboard to check the other driver's airway, counting aloud to keep the pulse steady, applying pressure to a gash that will not stop. He watches the silence swallow the arriving sirens, feels the quiet realization that the body beneath his palms has gone still while his own heart hammers against his ribs like a trapped bird. He had spent thirty years as a military medic, stabilizing men in burning vehicles and pulling them onto choppers under fire. A highway wreck should feel like another Tuesday in the grand calculus of survival. Instead, it becomes a wound that refuses to scar. For years after, he tells himself he has handled it. But the calculus stops working at home. The first year, he parks three blocks from the grocery store, his knuckles white on the steering wheel, watching every passing sedan as if it carries a ghost. He stops driving altogether, trading the wheel for long, measured walks along the creek behind his house. He keeps the house exactly as it was, though Eleanor's things sit in boxes he refuses to open, as if unpacking them would unravel the last thread holding him to her. She has been gone five years, yet the silence she leaves behind feels indistinguishable from the silence in the wrecked car. Now, at sixty-seven, the crash no longer arrives as a single event. It leaks into him. He wakes at 3 a.m., not to an alarm, but to the phantom rhythm of a monitor flatlining in his head. He sits on the edge of his bed, listening to the house breathe, wondering if the draft under the door is the same one that rushed through the shattered windshield that night. He works in his garage, restoring old tools, methodical and quiet. The precision of a wrench turning a bolt grounds him, but any sudden car backfiring on the street makes his shoulders lock, his breath shallow, his eyes scanning the horizon for a shape he has not seen in a decade. He tells himself it is just age, just the quiet of being alone. But when he watches the news, his thumb hovers over the remote, unable to press pause on traffic reports. He turns it off. He pours coffee. He stares at the window. When he sits in the chair across from me, his posture is straight, the kind of alignment drilled into him decades ago. He speaks in measured sentences, describing a life built on routine and restraint. He notices the rain against my office glass. He does not flinch, but his fingers tap a slow, steady rhythm on his knee-the same count he used to track a bleeding soldier's pulse. He talks about the garden he plants along the fence line, about how the soil does not care about speed limits or shattered glass. He pauses, watching a siren fade into the distance, and says the world moves too fast for him now. He does not look away from the window. He just sits there, breathing through the space between the memory and the morning.
